v: Calgary's proposed budget asks existing properties for fifteen percent more property tax next year. But your bill won't simply rise fifteen percent. Here's what our new study found.

The proposal is fifteen percent in twenty twenty-seven, then ten, seven point seven and six percent. Compounded, that is about forty-four percent more by twenty thirty. A typical home would pay about thirty-seven dollars a month more in City tax next year.

Population growth plus inflation adds up to about sixteen percent over the same four years. The proposed tax path is almost three times that benchmark. From twenty twenty-seven on, the tax steps move roughly in line with operating spending.

Where is spending growing? Water Services alone is forty-three percent of the operating increase, and it is paid mainly through water bills. Without water, City operating spending rises about nineteen percent from twenty twenty-seven to twenty thirty.

Every home shares one tax rate, so the tax follows value. Condo values have fallen faster than houses. As an estimate, a semi-detached home could see about eighteen percent, a detached house sixteen, and a condo apartment about eight. Give or take three points, until twenty twenty-seven assessments arrive in January.
This already showed up on this year's bills. Condo apartments lost about six percent of their assessed value, while detached houses gained almost one percent.

Calgary has about one point six million people, up about twenty-one percent since twenty twenty-one. On our ward model, five wards, five, twelve, thirteen, three and two, took about half of that growth.
Those five wards have about a third fewer transit stops per resident, and nearly three quarters fewer City recreation sites. These are counts of sites, not a measure of service quality.

What if Council chose ten percent instead? That is about one hundred twenty-eight million dollars less revenue in twenty twenty-seven. Five percent would be about two hundred fifty-six million less. These are revenue gaps, not a list of cuts.

Every figure comes from City open data, the full property assessment roll and the City's three hundred eighty-four budget requests, and it was checked by independent reviewers. The full study, with every source, is free at calgary insight dot c a.
Council debates the budget from November twenty-third. Is fifteen percent the right number? Tell us in the comments, and follow Calgary Insight for more.
